title: Notes Java Multithreading Using Runnable Interface

runs.text: Q1. What are the ways of creating threads in Java?

Ans: Independent instructions are executed by threads, and there are two ways to create the threads for them. In the first way the class that holds the instructions extends the Thread class. In the second way the class implements the Runnable interface. In
both ways the independent instructions are placed inside the run() method.
Q2. What is the Runnable interface?
Ans: Runnable is an interface of the java.lang package. It is a functional interface, which means that it has exactly one abstract method, and t
hat method is run(). A class that implements Runnable gives the body of run(), and the body contains the independent instructions that are to be executed in a thread.
Q3. What is the relationship between the Thread class and the Runnable interface?
Ans: Th

e Thread class itself implements the Runnable interface, and this is how the run() method is available in Thread. Opening the Thread class in an IDE such as Eclipse shows implements Runnable in its declaration. The Thread class also has a constructor that
accepts a reference of a Runnable object, so any object of a class that implements Runnable can be handed over to a Thread object.
Q4. How is a class changed from extending Thread to implementing Runnable?
Ans: Only the declaration changes. The words exten

ds Thread are replaced with implements Runnable, and the run() method with its independent instructions stays the same. For example, class PrintingNumbers extends Thread becomes class PrintingNumbers implements Runnable. The word implements means that the
class provides the body for the abstract method of the interface. Since the class no longer extends Thread, it does not inherit anything from the Thread class, including the start() method.
Q5. Why can start() not be called on an object of a class that onl
y implements Runnable?

Ans: start() is a method of the Thread class, and a class gets it only by inheriting from Thread. A class that implements Runnable has just the run() method and does not inherit start(), so calling start() on its object is a compile-
time error.
Sample Input: No input
Sample Output:
StartError.java:11: error: cannot find symbol
symbol:   method start()
location: variable pn of type PrintingNumbers
1 error
The object of PrintingNumbers is not a thread. A Thread object is needed to r
un it.
Q6. What are the steps for achieving multithreading?

Ans: There are four steps. Step 1 is to identify the independent instructions that have to execute at the same time. Step 2 is to put those instructions inside the run() method, either by extending the Thread class or by implementing the Runnable interface

. Step 3 is to create the thread, which has a small stack of its own: this is done by creating an object of the class that extends Thread, or, when the class only implements Runnable, by creating a Thread object. Step 4 is to call start() on the thread obj
ect, so that the thread begins to execute run().
Q7. How is a thread created when the class does not extend Thread?
Ans: A Thread object is created directly and the Runnable object is passed to its constructor. Thread is an ordinary class, so its object ca

n be created directly, in the same way as objects of String, StringBuffer, StringBuilder and Scanner. For example, Thread t1 = new Thread(pc); creates a thread for the Runnable object referred to by pc. The class name Thread starts with a capital letter, a
s class names always do. If the first option, an object of a class that extends Thread, is not possible, this second option is used.
Q8. Write a Java program that creates two threads by implementing the Runnable interface, one printing characters and the o
ther printing numbers.

Ans: PrintingCharacters and PrintingNumbers implement Runnable, and each holds its independent instructions in run(). In main, an object of each class is created, a Thread object is created for each of them, and start() is called on
the Thread objects.
Sample Input: No input
Sample Output (one possible run):
A
B
C
D
E

The two threads run concurrently, so the lines of the characters and the numbers can appear in a different order, or mixed together, in different runs. The order inside each thread does not change: the characters always come as A to E and the numbers as 1
to 5.
Q9. What happens when start() is called on a Thread object that was created with a Runnable object?
Ans: The thread gets its own stack, and the run() method of the Runnable object that was passed to the Thread constructor is executed on that stack. T

he run() method of the Thread class calls the run() method of the Runnable object. In the program above, the run() frame of PrintingCharacters is placed in the stack of t1, and the run() frame of PrintingNumbers is placed in the stack of t2.
Q10. What happ
ens in memory when a program creates threads using Runnable objects?
Ans: The program starts with the main stack, and the main method frame is placed in it. Objects are created in the heap. The statements new PrintingCharacters() and new PrintingNumbers()

create objects in the heap only. These classes implement Runnable and do not extend Thread, so no new stack comes with these objects. The statements new Thread(pc) and new Thread(pn) create two Thread objects in the heap, and each of them represents a thre

ad with a small stack of its own, apart from the main stack. The variables t1 and t2 refer to these Thread objects. After start() is called on them, the run() frames are placed in their stacks. The main stack and the two small stacks are then executed conc
urrently. When the first way is used, the object of the class that extends Thread is itself the thread, and the small stack comes with that object.
Q11. How is the time of a process shared among its threads, and what is concurrency?
Ans: A process gets a f

ixed amount of execution time, and that time is divided among its threads. For example, if a process has 20 seconds and four threads, each thread gets 5 seconds. When the time of a thread is over, it is stopped and the next thread is given its turn. The st

opped thread gets its turn again later and continues from the point where it stopped. This switching happens so fast that the threads seem to run at the same time. This way of executing is called concurrent execution, and multithreading is therefore also c
alled concurrent programming. Because the switching is decided by the system, the order in which the statements of different threads are printed can change between runs.
Q12. What happens to the other threads when an exception occurs in one thread?
Ans: In

a program that has only one thread, an unhandled exception terminates the program abruptly. When there are several threads, an exception that occurs in one thread terminates only that thread. The other threads continue to work and execute, because threads
are independent of each other. Each thread has its own stack and its own independent instructions.
Q13. Write a program in which one Runnable thread throws an exception by dividing by zero while another thread prints numbers.
Ans: DivisionTask divides num1 by num2, which is 0, so run() throws an ArithmeticException in its thread. PrintingNumbers is in another thread and is not affected.
Sample Input: No input
Sample Output (one possible run):
Exception in thread "Thread-0" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
at Divis
ionTask.run(ExceptionDemo.java:5)

The stack trace continues with lines of the JDK classes, which depend on the Java version, and the position of the exception message among the numbers can differ between runs. The thread running DivisionTask dies, and the thread that prints numbers still p
rints all its numbers from 1 to 5.
